messages.subject: Amplitude change after cutw
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Seewave is great -- but I've noticed some strange behavior that probably has a simple answer. I use this for a very quick batch loading and trimming of segments of WAV files in the following workflow:

I import the WAV file using: input <- readWave("filename.wav")
I then use cutw to trim out a section of the WAV file: clip <- cutw(input, from=start, to=stop, output="Wave")
I then use: clip <- normalize(clip, unit="16")
Lastly: writeWave(clip,"clipped_file.wav")

It works perfectly, except the clipped WAV file has a much greater amplitude than that segment in the original file when I want it to have the exact same spectral characteristics as the original unclipped file. I'm sure there's something simple I'm missing -- any ideas?

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: Amplitude change after cutw
messages.body_plain:
>From what I understand, when you use the normalize function, you normalize (or adjust) the amplitude of that clip with respect to the loudest portion of it.  So if the clipped portion of the file is quieter than the rest of the file, when you clip it out and normalize it, it will increase the amplitude.

Seewave is a great package, and has a lot great things it can do.  However, I've found that it can be a bit slow when it comes to manipulating song files (cutting, trimming, etc.)  My preference now is to use a combo of seewave and sox within R to manipulate and extract info from my sound files.  Sox is a command line program that you can call from R (although I admit, I can't see to get it working in Windows 7, although I have no problem with Ubuntu)

For example:

input <- "filename.wav"
output <- "clipped_file.wav"
from <- 5
to <- 10
system(paste("sox",input,output,"trim",from,to))

If my memory serves, this command doesn't include any normalization, so the amplitudes should be consistent.

Enjoy!

Steffi LaZerte

messages.subject: submitting documentation fixes
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

As I learn more about seewave, I've occasionally been finding errors
in the documentation. Some are simple typoes and such, but a few of
them are capable of causing confusion. For example, the autoc()
example doesn't currently work; it has

res<-autoc(sheep, f=8000, threshold=5, fmin=100, fmax=700)

where it should have

res<-autoc(sheep, f=8000, threshold=5, fmin=100, fmax=700, plot=FALSE)

What is the right way to report this sort of thing? I'd like to be
able to help fix things when I notice them, but I don't necessarily
want to clog up this google group every time I see a typo.

Thanks very much,
Jesse Ross

messages.subject_clean: problems with listen parameter on noisew()
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm having trouble with the listen parameter on noisew(). Here is a mini-session:

> foo = noisew(44100, 1, output="Wave")   # works fine
> listen(foo)  # plays fine
> foo = noisew(44100, 1, output="Wave", listen=T)   # does not work!
Error in is.data.frame(wave) : object 'sound' not found

The listen parameter on synth() works fine though:

> foo = synth(44100, 1, 1000, output="Wave", listen=T)   # creates wav and plays it

I'm using R 2.15.0 on Windows, with seewave 1.6.3. I'm using sox "play.exe" as my sound player.

Thanks very much,
Jesse Ross

Hello,

If you wish to save the spectrogram matrix, do something like this

data(tico)
spectro <- spectro(tico, plot=FALSE)$amp
write.table(spectro, file="spectro.txt", row.names=FALSE, col.names=FALSE)

Best regards

Jerome

Hi Arjun,

Do you know about the help system in R? It is a great way to get pretty complete information about any function. One of the things that makes R really special is how good and complete the documentation tends to be. For instance, try

help("data")

This can be abbreviated to the question mark, like

?help
?spectro
?("$")

If the combination of ?("$") and the "Value" section of ?spectro don't clarify the use of $amp in Jerome's code sample, it would be worthwhile to work through an R tutorial such as  http://www.cyclismo.org/tutorial/R/ . The dollar sign operator is quite common.

Best,
Jesse Ross
